source: MAFF/partner document, "ដំណំពោត" (Corn Crop), Section I: Status of corn in Cambodia
text:
Corn is a crop that has been grown in Cambodia since the 17th century, first cultivated on small plots as a supplementary food alongside other staples. It rose in national economic importance starting in 1910, when the French began importing large quantities of corn from abroad, and later encouraged local growing of corn under their supervision to be used as animal feed.

All the earliest corn grown in Cambodia belonged to the flint or waxy/soft corn type, with a short growth cycle of about 90 days. This everyday corn (also called sticky/glutinous-type corn) was traditionally boiled, roasted, grilled, or made into various sweets and desserts, and became a form of local/rural commerce between neighboring villages.

Sweet corn, by contrast, came from Hong Kong and South America; afterward, a Khmer red corn variety was developed by the Ministry of Agriculture's plant breeding work during the 1930s. This tall Khmer red corn also had a short growth cycle of about 90 days, with a fairly small, tapered ear about 20 cm long, medium-to-small kernel rows (fewer than 8 rows), and kernels colored either dark yellow/orange or red, with uniform kernel rows and no gaps, which made the variety valuable in the market. Breeding efforts to improve this variety further were carried out in Phnom Penh and in Kampong Cham province.
